claim: Human reproduction is controlled by ~2000 hypothalamic gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) neurons.
source: Human reproduction is controlled by ~2000 hypothalamic gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction referencing established scientific knowledge about GnRH neuron numbers.

claim: The human basal ganglia and basal forebrain contain ~150,000–200,000 GnRH-synthesizing cells.
source: Here, we report the discovery and characterization of additional ~150,000–200,000 GnRH-synthesizing cells in the human basal ganglia and basal forebrain.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis data presented in the Results section where cell counts were performed on three subjects.

claim: Nearly all extrahypothalamic GnRH neurons expressed the cholinergic marker enzyme choline acetyltransferase.
source: Nearly all extrahypothalamic GnRH neurons expressed the cholinergic marker enzyme choline acetyltransferase.
evidence: This is supported by dual-immunofluorescence experiments showing colocalization of GnRH and ChAT, as described in the Results section and shown in Figure 1G-I.

claim: Hypothalamic GnRH neurons were cholinergic both in embryonic and adult human brains.
source: Similarly, hypothalamic GnRH neurons were also cholinergic both in embryonic and adult human brains.
evidence: This is supported by dual-immunofluorescence data from adult brains (Figure 3A-B) and fetal tissues at GW11 (Figure 3C-E).

claim: Cholinergic interneurons of the human putamen selectively express GNRH1 and GNRHR1 autoreceptors.
source: Whole-transcriptome analysis of cholinergic interneurons and medium spiny projection neurons laser-microdissected from the human putamen showed selective expression of GNRH1 and GNRHR1 autoreceptors in the cholinergic cell population
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing GNRH1 and GNRHR1 expression exclusively in ChIN pools, as shown in Figure 4C and described in the Results.

claim: Mammalian reproduction is controlled by a few hundred/thousand preoptic/hypothalamic neurons that release GnRH into the hypophysial portal circulation.
source: Mammalian reproduction is controlled by a few hundred/thousand preoptic/hypothalamic neurons, which release the decapeptide neurohormone gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) into the hypophysial portal circulation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Herbison, 2018, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: GnRH promotes fertility via increasing the synthesis and secretion of luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone in the anterior pituitary.
source: GnRH promotes fertility via increasing the synthesis and secretion of luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone in the anterior pituitary (Herbison, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Herbison, 2018, representing established scientific knowledge about GnRH function.

claim: GnRH neurons are born in the olfactory placodes and migrate into the forebrain prenatally.
source: Unlike other neurons of the central nervous system, GnRH neurons are born in the olfactory placodes and migrate into the forebrain prenatally (Casoni et al., 2016; Schwanzel-Fukuda and Pfaff, 1989; Wray et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies establishing the developmental origin of GnRH neurons.

claim: Approximately 2000 GnRH neurons were observed along a ventral migratory path to the hypothalamus in human embryos/fetuses.
source: Approximately 2000 neurons were observed along a ventral migratory path whereby GnRH neurons reach the hypothalamus to regulate reproduction after puberty.
evidence: This is based on developmental studies by Casoni et al., 2016, cited in the introduction.

claim: A dorsal migratory route has been identified whereby ~8000 GnRH neurons migrated towards pallial and/or subpallial structures in human development.
source: In addition, a previously unknown dorsal migratory route has been identified whereby ~8000 GnRH neurons migrated towards pallial and/or subpallial structures.
evidence: This is based on developmental studies by Casoni et al., 2016, cited in the introduction.

claim: GnRH neurons in adult laboratory rodents are mostly preoptic/hypothalamic and serve reproductive functions.
source: While GnRH neurons in adult laboratory rodents are mostly preoptic/hypothalamic and serve reproductive functions (Merchenthaler et al., 1980)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Merchenthaler et al., 1980, representing established knowledge about rodent GnRH neurons.

claim: Primates have additional GNRH1 mRNA expression and/or GnRH immunoreactivity in extrahypothalamic regions including basal ganglia and basal forebrain.
source: a handful of anatomical studies on primates identified additional GNRH1 mRNA expression and/or GnRH immunoreactivity in extrahypothalamic regions unrelated to reproduction. These included several basal ganglia and the basal forebrain (Krajewski et al., 2003; Quanbeck et al., 1997; Rance et al., 1994; Terasawa et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous anatomical studies on primates.

claim: Extrahypothalamic GnRH neurons in monkeys were suggested to contain the GnRH degradation product GnRH1-5, instead of the bona fide GnRH decapeptide.
source: Initial enthusiasm to study these neurons further faded after suggestions that extrahypothalamic GnRH neurons in monkeys contain the GnRH degradation product GnRH1-5, instead of the bona fide GnRH decapeptide (Quanbeck et al., 1997; Terasawa et al., 2001).
evidence: This is based on previous studies cited (Quanbeck et al., 1997; Terasawa et al., 2001).

claim: The majority (82.2%) of the 163,168 ± 36,223 extrahypothalamic GnRH neurons occurred in the putamen.
source: 82.2 ± 1.1% of labeled cells were observed in the Pu
evidence: This is supported by quantitative cell counting data from three subjects, as shown in Figure 1C and described in the Results.

claim: Extrahypothalamic GnRH-immunoreactive neurons occur in the putamen, nucleus accumbens, nucleus caudatus, nucleus basalis magnocellularis, globus pallidus, ventral pallidum, and bed nucleus of the stria terminalis.
source: This experiment revealed numerous extrahypothalamic GnRH-IR neurons in the Pu, moderate numbers in the nucleus accumbens (nAcc) and the head of the nucleus caudatus (Cd), and lower numbers also in the nbM (Figure 1C). Labeled neurons were also scattered in the globus pallidus (GP), the ventral pallidum (VP), and the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BnST).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry mapping data shown in Figure 1 and described in the Results.

claim: GnRH-immunoreactive perikarya in the putamen showed round or oval shape, with a mean diameter of 29 µm.
source: The immunostained perikarya showed round or oval shape, with a mean diameter of 29 µm in the Pu (Figure 1B, C).
evidence: This is based on morphological measurements from immunostained sections.

claim: Preabsorption of the GnRH antiserum with 0.1 µg/ml GnRH decapeptide eliminated all labeling in control experiments.
source: Preabsorption of the working solution of this antiserum with 0.1 µg/ml GnRH decapeptide eliminated all labeling in control experiments using sections of three subjects (#17–19) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a negative control experiment demonstrating antibody specificity, as shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The total number of extrahypothalamic GnRH neurons in three adult human brains was 229,447, 155,357, and 104,699.
source: The total number of extrahypothalamic GnRH neurons calculated this way in three subjects was 229,447 (31-year-old female; #1), 155,357 (61-year-old male; #2), and 104,699 (62-year-old male; #3) (163,168 ± 36,223; mean ± SEM).
evidence: This is based on stereological cell counting with Abercrombie's correction factor applied to three subjects.

claim: The high GnRH cell numbers make it unlikely that human extrahypothalamic GnRH neurons develop from olfactory placodes and migrate into the brain along the dorsal migratory route.
source: These unexpectedly high GnRH cell numbers made it unlikely that human extrahypothalamic GnRH neurons develop from olfactory placodes and migrate into the brain along the dorsal migratory route (Casoni et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the discrepancy between the ~8000 neurons observed in the dorsal migratory route during development and the much larger numbers found in adults.

claim: All tested GnRH and GAP1 antibodies, including the LR-1 antiserum, recognized GnRH-IR neurons in the human putamen.
source: All of the tested antibodies, including the LR-1 antiserum, recognized GnRH-IR neurons (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry experiments testing multiple antibodies, as shown in Figure 2B.

claim: GnRH-immunoreactive neurons express GNRH1 mRNA.
source: Results of further control experiments with the combined use of IF and non-isotopic ISH (N = 5; #15–19) showed that GnRH-IR neurons express GNRH1 mRNA (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on combined immunofluorescence and in situ hybridization experiments, as shown in Figure 2D.

claim: HPLC-MS/MS detects bona fide GnRH decapeptide in tissue extracts from the mediobasal hypothalamus, putamen, and nucleus caudatus, but not the claustrum.
source: HPLC-MS/MS analysis of the tissue extracts established that the dominant peptide form in the Pu and Cd is the GnRH decapeptide. GnRH1-5 was also present, albeit at 3–4 times lower tissue concentrations (Figure 2E–G). Only GnRH decapeptide was detectable in the MBH (used as a positive control) where hypophysiotropic GnRH neurons occur and neither peptide form was present in the Cl
evidence: This is based on HPLC-MS/MS analysis of tissue extracts from multiple brain regions, as shown in Figure 2E-G.

claim: GnRH1-5 is present in the putamen and nucleus caudatus at 3-4 times lower tissue concentrations than GnRH decapeptide.
source: GnRH1-5 was also present, albeit at 3–4 times lower tissue concentrations (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: This is based on quantitative HPLC-MS/MS measurements, as shown in Figure 2F-G.

claim: Extrahypothalamic GnRH neurons mainly produce bona fide GnRH decapeptide derived from the GNRH1 gene.
source: Together with observations from the IHC and ISH experiments, HPLC-MS/MS results gave firm support to the notion that extrahypothalamic GnRH neurons mainly produce bona fide GnRH decapeptide derived from the GNRH1 gene.
evidence: This conclusion is based on multiple lines of evidence including IHC, ISH, and HPLC-MS/MS data.

claim: DiI-labeled GnRH neurons in the putamen are large multipolar cells with poorly spined dendrites.
source: Confocal microscopic analysis and 3-D reconstruction of the DiI signal revealed spider-like neurons with rich arborization of poorly spined dendrites.
evidence: This is based on DiI labeling and confocal microscopy analysis, as shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: DiI-labeled GnRH neurons are clearly distinct from medium spiny GABAergic projection neurons.
source: DiI-labeled GnRH neurons were clearly distinct from the main Pu cell type, the densely spined medium spiny GABAergic projection neurons (SPNs) (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: This is based on morphological comparison using DiI labeling and confocal microscopy, as shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: The vast majority of extrahypothalamic GnRH neurons are cholinergic.
source: The extent of ChAT/GnRH colocalization was assessed quantitatively in five distinct regions of a 62-year-old male subject (#3). Confocal microscopic analysis of representative dual-labeled sections established that the vast majority of extrahypothalamic GnRH neurons are cholinergic (green bars in Figure 1I).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of dual-immunofluorescence experiments, as shown in Figure 1I.

claim: GnRH-immunoreactive neurons represented 34.9% of all cholinergic neurons in the putamen.
source: In contrast, GnRH-IR neurons represented only 34.9% of all cholinergic neurons in the Pu
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of dual-immunofluorescence experiments, as shown in Figure 1I.

claim: 34.6 ± 7.1% of hypothalamic GnRH neurons exhibited ChAT signal in seven adult human subjects.
source: Unexpectedly, 34.6 ± 7.1% of the hypothalamic GnRH neurons also exhibited ChAT signal in seven adult human male and female subjects (Figure 3A, B; #3 and 6–11)
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of dual-immunofluorescence experiments on hypothalamic sections from seven subjects, as shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: The cholinergic phenotype of GnRH neurons has not been observed in other species before.
source: a phenomenon not observed in other species before.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding and is supported by the lack of previous reports in the literature.

claim: At gestational week 11, GnRH-positive neurons within the nasal compartment did not contain ChAT signal.
source: While GnRH-positive neurons within the nasal compartment did not contain ChAT signal (Figure 3C)
evidence: This is based on dual-immunofluorescence experiments on fetal tissues at GW11, as shown in Figure 3C.

claim: At gestational week 11, GnRH neurons in the septum, striatum and elsewhere in the developing brain were already ChAT-immunoreactive.
source: those in the septum (Figure 3D), the striatum (Figure 3E) and elsewhere in the developing brain were already ChAT-IR.
evidence: This is based on dual-immunofluorescence experiments on fetal tissues at GW11, as shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: Migrating GnRH neurons become cholinergic after entering the brain and continue to express ChAT immunoreactivity in hypothalamic as well as extrahypothalamic regions.
source: These data suggest that migrating GnRH neurons become cholinergic after entering the brain and continue to express ChAT immunoreactivity in hypothalamic as well as extrahypothalamic regions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the developmental time course of ChAT expression observed in fetal tissues.

claim: Each ChIN-enriched pool contained ~300 large neurons and each SPN-enriched pool consisted of ~600 medium-sized neurons.
source: Each ChIN-enriched pool contained ~300 large neurons and each SPN-enriched pool consisted of ~600 medium-sized neurons (Figure 4A).
evidence: This describes the laser-capture microdissection protocol used for RNA-seq experiments.

claim: 29.4M and 25.8M reads were obtained from the two ChIN pools and 26.3M and 3.2M reads from the two SPN pools.
source: 29.4M and 25.8M reads were obtained from the two ChIN pools and 26.3M and 3.2M reads from the two SPN pools.
evidence: This reports the RNA-sequencing output from the four cell pools.

claim: Cholinergic markers including CHAT, SLC5A7, SLC18A3, ACHE, and CHRM2 were highly enriched in the ChIN pools.
source: Cholinergic markers, including CHAT, SLC5A7, SLC18A3, ACHE, and CHRM2, were highly enriched in the ChIN pools from subjects #21 and 22. These transcripts were either absent or found at low levels only in the two SPN pools (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data showing differential expression of cholinergic markers, as shown in Figure 4B.

claim: LIM transcripts (LHX8, ISL1, and GBX2) as well as type 3 vesicular glutamate transporter (SLC17A8) showed robust and exclusive expression in ChINs.
source: These LIM transcripts as well as type 3 vesicular glutamate transporter (SLC17A8) showed robust and exclusive expression in ChINs (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data, as shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The SPN pools expressed much higher levels of known SPN markers than ChINs, including CHRM1, HTR6, GRM1, DRD1, TAC1, PDYN, and PENK.
source: The SPN pools, in turn, expressed much higher levels of known SPN markers than ChINs, including various cholinergic (CHRM1), serotonergic (HTR6), glutamatergic (GRM1), and dopaminergic (DRD1) receptor isoforms and several neuropeptides (TAC1, PDYN, PENK) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data showing differential expression of SPN markers, as shown in Figure 4B.

claim: ChINs express GABAergic marker transcripts (GAD1, GAD2, SLC6A1, and SLC32A1) in addition to SPNs.
source: Relatively high levels of expression of known GABAergic marker transcripts (GAD1, GAD2, SLC6A1, and SLC32A1) in ChINs, in addition to SPNs (Figure 4B), revealed that ChINs use GABAergic co-transmission, as proposed earlier for ChINs of the rodent CPU (Lozovaya et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data showing GABAergic marker expression in ChINs, as shown in Figure 4B, and is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: GNRH1 was expressed exclusively in the two ChIN pools.
source: GNRH1 was expressed exclusively in the two ChIN pools, in accordance with the morphological observations (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data showing selective GNRH1 expression in ChINs, as shown in Figure 4C.

claim: ChINs abundantly expressed the PCSK2 prohormone convertase isoform.
source: Processing of the proGnRH1 protein begins with endoproteolysis by prohormone convertases from which ChINs abundantly expressed the PCSK2 isoform.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data, as shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Enzymes catalyzing subsequent steps of GnRH biosynthesis, including CPE, CPD, PAM, and QPCT, were present in ChINs.
source: Enzymes catalyzing subsequent steps of GnRH biosynthesis, including carboxypeptidases (CPE, CPD), peptidylglycine α-amidating monooxygenase (PAM), and glutaminyl cyclase enzymes (QPCT), were also present in ChINs (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data showing expression of GnRH biosynthetic enzymes, as shown in Figure 4C.

claim: THOP1 enzyme was expressed in both ChINs and SPNs, with a higher relative abundance in SPNs.
source: The promiscuous THOP1 enzyme accounts for the cleavage of multiple neuropeptides, including GnRH. This enzyme was expressed in both ChINs and SPNs, with a higher relative abundance in the latter.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data, as shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The seven-transmembrane receptor GNRHR1 was expressed selectively in ChINs.
source: The most important finding of the RNA-seq study was that the seven-transmembrane receptor GNRHR1 was expressed selectively in ChINs.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data showing selective GNRHR1 expression in ChINs, as shown in Figure 4C.

claim: GnRH in the human putamen acts on GnRHR1 autoreceptors.
source: This observation indicated that GnRH in the human Pu acts on GnRHR1 autoreceptors
evidence: This is an inference based on the selective expression of both GNRH1 and GNRHR1 in ChINs.

claim: It is unlikely that SPNs are affected directly by GnRH derived from ChINs.
source: and also made it unlikely that SPNs are affected directly by GnRH derived from ChINs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of GNRHR1 expression in SPNs.

claim: GnRH is synthesized by ChINs and acts locally via GnRHR1 autoreceptors.
source: Altogether, transcriptome profiling of ChINs and SPNs provided molecular support to a concept that GnRH is synthesized by ChINs and acts locally via GnRHR1 autoreceptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined RNA-seq data showing GNRH1 and GNRHR1 expression in ChINs.

claim: Extrahypothalamic GnRH-IR neurons correspond to type III GnRH neurons detected earlier with in situ hybridization.
source: The GnRH-IR neurons we detected in our study correspond to type III neurons characterized by round/oval shape, large nucleus and nucleolus, prominent Nissl substance, and GNRH1 mRNA levels intermediate between those of heavily labeled type I neurons in the MBH and lightly labeled type II neurons in the medial septum and the dorsal medial preoptic area (Rance et al., 1994).
evidence: This is based on comparison with previous ISH studies by Rance et al., 1994.

claim: Type III GnRH neurons have not been reported in adult laboratory rodents.
source: Although type III GnRH neurons have not been reported in adult laboratory rodents, they occur in the striatum, amygdala, and nbM of non-human primates (Krajewski et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on the absence of reports in the literature and is supported by citation to primate studies.

claim: The human genome includes a fully functional GNRH2 gene, in addition to GNRH1.
source: We note that the human genome includes a fully functional GNRH2 gene (Stewart et al., 2009), in addition to GNRH1.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stewart et al., 2009.

claim: The GnRH signals detected in the putamen are due to GNRH1, rather than GNRH2 expression.
source: The GnRH signals we detected in the Pu are due to GNRH1, rather than GNRH2 expression, because (1) extrahypothalamic GnRH-IR neurons also exhibit ISH signal for GNRH1 mRNA, (2) they are IR to GAP1, which only has low homology with the corresponding GAP2 sequence, and (3) ChINs of the Pu express high levels of the GNRH1 transcript, according to RNA-seq results.
evidence: This is based on multiple lines of evidence including ISH, immunoreactivity to GAP1, and RNA-seq data.

claim: GPR101 was expressed at high levels in SPNs (mean cpm: 58.4) and at low levels in ChINs (mean cpm: 6.4).
source: Transcriptomic studies revealed that one of the putative GnRH1-5 receptors, GPR101 (Cho-Clark et al., 2014), was expressed at high levels in SPNs (mean cpm: 58.4) and at low levels in ChINs (mean cpm: 6.4) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data from the transcriptome analysis.

claim: If GnRH1-5 is a physiological neurotransmitter of human ChINs, it may regulate SPNs via GPR101.
source: This differential expression suggests that if GnRH1-5 is a physiological neurotransmitter of human ChINs, it may regulate SPNs via GPR101.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the differential expression of GPR101 in SPNs versus ChINs.

claim: Bona fide hypothalamic GnRH neurons in the developing monkey brain exhibited THOP1 immunoreactivity.
source: Moreover, bona fide hypothalamic GnRH neurons in the developing monkey brain also exhibited THOP1 immunoreactivity (Terasawa et al., 2001).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous work by Terasawa et al., 2001.

claim: Total GnRH-IR cell numbers calculated for the basal forebrain and basal ganglia exceeded all previous estimates of GnRH cell numbers in any species.
source: Total GnRH-IR cell numbers we calculated for the basal forebrain and the basal ganglia of three adult human brains (229,447, 155,357, and 104,699) exceeded all previous estimates of GnRH cell numbers in any species.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on the quantitative data from this study and knowledge of previous literature.

claim: The placodal origin of extrahypothalamic GnRH neurons is very unlikely considering the much larger GnRH cell numbers observed in the adult brain.
source: Our initial hypothesis was that extrahypothalamic GnRH neurons are derived from the ~8000 GnRH neurons reported recently along the dorsal migratory route during embryonic/fetal development (Casoni et al., 2016). The placodal origin now seems to be very unlikely considering the much larger GnRH cell numbers we observed in the adult brain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discrepancy between developmental and adult cell numbers.

claim: Extrahypothalamic GnRH neurons of the human central nervous system appear to be homologous to the 'early type' GnRH neurons reported in the developing monkey embryo and fetus.
source: Extrahypothalamic GnRH neurons of the human central nervous system also appear to be homologous to the 'early type' GnRH neurons reported in the developing monkey embryo and fetus (Quanbeck et al., 1997).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with previous studies on monkey development, supported by citation.

claim: A 10- to 10,000-fold increase in the number of 'early' GnRH neurons in the basal forebrain within just a few days indicates that early GnRH neurons might be derived from the ventricular wall of the telencephalic vesicle.
source: However, in a subsequent study these authors noted that a 10- to 10,000-fold increase in the number of 'early' GnRH neurons in the basal forebrain within just a few days indicates that early GnRH neurons might rather be derived from the ventricular wall of the telencephalic vesicle (Terasawa et al., 2001).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous work by Terasawa et al., 2001.

claim: The possibility of non-placodal GnRH neuron development is compatible with the in vitro capability of hypothalamic and hippocampal progenitors to generate GnRH cells.
source: The possibility of non-placodal GnRH neuron development is compatible with the in vitro capability of hypothalamic and hippocampal progenitors to generate GnRH cells and all other neuroendocrine cell types (Markakis et al., 2004).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous work by Markakis et al., 2004.

claim: ChINs exhibit substantial diversity in their physiology, morphology, and connectivity.
source: It is worth noting that our RNA-seq studies provided transcriptomic information about a mixed ChIN population of the Pu, whereas ChINs exhibit substantial diversity in their physiology, morphology, and connectivity (Gonzales and Smith, 2015).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous work by Gonzales and Smith, 2015.

claim: ChIN subclasses differ in their developmental origin (medial ganglionic eminence, septal epithelium, or preoptic area) and transcription factor profiles.
source: Subclasses differ in their developmental origin (medial ganglionic eminence, septal epithelium, or preoptic area) and transcription factor profiles (Ahmed et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous work by Ahmed et al., 2019.

claim: Rodent GnRH neurons are regulated by cholinergic afferents but not known to co-express cholinergic markers.
source: Rodent GnRH neurons are regulated by cholinergic afferents but not known to co-express cholinergic markers (Turi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous work by Turi et al., 2008.

claim: The cholinergic phenotype of GnRH neurons is a true species difference between humans and rodents.
source: The lack of success of this attempt (Skrapits et al., unpublished) suggests that the cholinergic phenotype of GnRH neurons is a true species difference between humans and rodents.
evidence: This is an inference based on unsuccessful attempts to detect ChAT in mouse GnRH neurons.

claim: GNRHR1 mRNA and immunoreactivity were reported in pyramidal neurons of the human hippocampus and cerebral cortex.
source: High levels of GNRHR1 mRNA and immunoreactivity were reported in pyramidal neurons of the human hippocampus and cerebral cortex (Wilson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous work by Wilson et al., 2006.

claim: GnRH analogues were anti-apoptotic in a rat model of ischemia/reperfusion.
source: GnRH analogues were anti-apoptotic in a rat model of ischemia/reperfusion (Chu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous work by Chu et al., 2010.

claim: GnRH increased hippocampal estradiol levels and the spontaneous firing and GNRHR1 expression of pyramidal neurons and prevented memory deficits caused by amyloid β deposition.
source: Further, GnRH increased hippocampal estradiol levels and the spontaneous firing and GNRHR1 expression of pyramidal neurons and prevented memory deficits caused by amyloid β deposition (Marbouti et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous work by Marbouti et al., 2020.

claim: GnRHR1 in ChINs of the basal ganglia can bind locally synthesized GnRH neuropeptide.
source: While the source of GnRH acting on hippocampal neurons remains to be explored, results of our studies indicate that GnRHR1 in ChINs of the basal ganglia can bind locally synthesized GnRH neuropeptide.
evidence: This is an inference based on the coexpression of GNRH1 and GNRHR1 in ChINs.

claim: ChINs of the striatum contribute as interneurons to the regulation of cortico-striato-thalamocortical neural pathways.
source: ChINs of the striatum contribute as interneurons to the regulation of cortico-striato-thalamocortical neural pathways.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about striatal circuitry.

claim: Functions associated with cortico-striato-thalamocortical circuitry include motor control, learning, language, reward, cognitive function, and addiction.
source: Functions associated with this circuitry include motor control, learning, language, reward, cognitive function, and addiction (Fazl and Fleisher, 2018).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous work by Fazl and Fleisher, 2018.

claim: Cholinergic neurons of the nucleus basalis of Meynert project to the entire cortical mantle, olfactory tubercle, and amygdala.
source: Cholinergic neurons of the nbM, which project to the entire cortical mantle, olfactory tubercle, and amygdala
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about nbM projections, supported by citation.

claim: Cholinergic neurons of the nucleus basalis of Meynert have been implicated in the control of attention, maintenance of arousal, and learning and memory formation.
source: have been implicated in the control of attention, maintenance of arousal, and learning and memory formation (Koulousakis et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous work by Koulousakis et al., 2019.

claim: Non-reproductive dysfunctions have not been characterized in GnRH-deficient patients.
source: Non-reproductive dysfunctions have not been characterized in GnRH-deficient patients (Chan, 2011)
evidence: This is based on citation to previous work by Chan, 2011.

claim: Non-reproductive dysfunctions have not been characterized in cases of GnRHR1 deficiency.
source: or in the more common cases of GnRHR1 deficiency (Chevrier et al., 2011; Seminara et al., 1998).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous work by Chevrier et al., 2011 and Seminara et al., 1998.

claim: Leading symptoms and cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease are due to the loss of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons.
source: Leading symptoms and cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease are due to the loss of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons many of which exhibited GnRH immunoreactivity in nbM.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Alzheimer's disease pathology.

claim: Many non-motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease can be explained with the loss of the nigrostriatal dopaminergic input.
source: Many of these malfunctions in PD can be explained with the loss of the nigrostriatal dopaminergic input and ameliorated with levodopa.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Parkinson's disease pathophysiology.

claim: Gait disorders and cognitive impairment/dementia in Parkinson's disease are most often unresponsive to dopamine precursor treatment.
source: However, gait disorders and cognitive impairment/dementia are most often unresponsive to dopamine precursor treatment.
evidence: This is based on established clinical knowledge about Parkinson's disease treatment.

claim: Loss of striatal dopamine input causes a local hypercholinergic state in the striatum.
source: In particular, loss of striatal dopamine input causes a local hypercholinergic state in the striatum with consequences reviewed recently (Tubert and Murer, 2021).
evidence: This is based on citation to a recent review by Tubert and Murer, 2021.

claim: The hypercholinergic state explains the success of early Parkinson's disease therapies with Atropa belladonna derivatives.
source: This hypercholinergic state explains the success of early PD therapies with Atropa belladonna derivatives (Goetz, 2011).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous work by Goetz, 2011.

claim: Selective inhibition of striatal ChINs has been proposed as a promising strategy to improve the transmitter balance in dopamine-deprived basal ganglia.
source: Although the low efficacy of anticholinergic drugs compared to levodopa and unwanted side effects limit the use of general anticholinergic strategies (Katzenschlager et al., 2003), selective inhibition of striatal ChINs has been proposed recently as a more promising strategy to improve the transmitter balance in dopamine-deprived basal ganglia (Mallet et al., 2019; Tubert and Murer, 2021).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous work by Mallet et al., 2019 and Tubert and Murer, 2021.

claim: Deletion of M2-type autoreceptors results in increased striatal acetylcholine release.
source: Accordingly, deletion of M2-type autoreceptors results in increased striatal acetylcholine release (Bonsi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous work by Bonsi et al., 2008.

claim: Autoinhibitory mechanism by muscarinic autoreceptors was found to be lost in Parkinson's disease animal models.
source: Autoinhibitory mechanism by muscarinic autoreceptors was found to be lost in PD animal models (Ding et al., 2006).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous work by Ding et al., 2006.

claim: Human ChINs contain very high levels of CHRM2 autoreceptors.
source: Indeed, our RNA-seq analysis confirmed that human ChINs contain very high levels of CHRM2 autoreceptors (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data, as shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Approximately 9.6M and 6.6M reads from ChIN pools were mapped to the GRCh38.p13 human reference genome.
